q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS COUNT FROM PRODUCT)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS COUNT FROM PRODUCT)
counterexample: INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2), (3); INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 2);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) in the HAVING clause, while Q2 uses COUNT(*) AS COUNT in the subquery. This difference in the subquery's COUNT function affects the results when the number of products is not the same as the number of customer-product pairs.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have a number of products that is different from the number of customer-product pairs. This will cause Q1 and Q2 to return different results.
